summary.text: A 42-year-old male with ileocolonic Crohn’s disease, diagnosed before liver transplantation for primary sclerosing cholangitis, started upadacitinib 30 mg/day for active IBD 0.9 years after the transplant. His prior IBD therapies were 5-aminosalicylate, prednisone, azathioprine, infliximab, adalimumab, vedolizumab and ustekinumab, and no prior Janus kinase inhibitor exposure was recorded.

At upadacitinib start he was on tacrolimus as anti-rejection therapy and prednisone 30 mg with ustekinumab, which was replaced by upadacitinib. The Harvey–Bradshaw Index fell from 14 to 1 at week 12 and he achieved steroid-free clinical remission within 12 weeks; an attempted taper from 30 to 15 mg/day was followed by continued remission.

No rejection and no adverse events were recorded, and there were no life-threatening adverse events. Upadacitinib was continued at the last follow-up after 12 months of exposure and 12 months of total follow-up. Upadacitinib decisions followed multidisciplinary discussion between IBD and transplant hepatologists, with risks and benefits explained.

summary.text: A 50-year-old female developed ileocolonic Crohn’s disease after liver transplantation for primary sclerosing cholangitis and started upadacitinib 30 mg/day for active IBD 11.6 years after the transplant, with a 2-year IBD duration. Tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisone 20 mg were in use, risankizumab was replaced by upadacitinib, and she had no prior Janus kinase inhibitor exposure.

The Harvey–Bradshaw Index fell from 8 to 3 at week 8 with steroid-free clinical remission within 12 weeks. She developed elevated liver function, with AST and ALT up to 83 and 228 U/L; liver biopsy at 3 months showed nonspecific findings with focal portal inflammation and mild bile duct injury without evidence of rejection.

Upadacitinib was continued given the significant response of her Crohn’s disease, and AST and ALT subsequently normalized without changing treatment. It was still continued at the last follow-up after 9 months of exposure and 9 months of follow-up. There were no life-threatening adverse events, and decisions followed multidisciplinary discussion with risks and benefits explained.

summary.text: A 41-year-old female with ileocolonic Crohn’s disease diagnosed before liver transplantation for primary sclerosing cholangitis started upadacitinib 15 mg/day 2.8 years after the transplant, with a 24-year IBD duration and many prior therapies. Mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, adalimumab and prednisone 10 mg were in use at the start, and no prior Janus kinase inhibitor exposure was recorded.

Within a month of starting upadacitinib, AST and ALT rose from 14 and 15 U/L up to 107 and 57 U/L, and subsequently normalized. Table 2 records elevated liver function tests as the adverse event and the reason for stopping upadacitinib, with efficacy not applicable because of early discontinuation and no rejection.

Upadacitinib was not continued at the last follow-up, after 1.5 months of exposure and 22.5 months of total follow-up. There were no life-threatening adverse events, and decisions about upadacitinib followed multidisciplinary discussion between IBD and transplant hepatologists, with risks and benefits explained.

summary.text: A 37-year-old male with ulcerative colitis (pancolitis, post proctocolectomy with ileal pouch anal anastomosis) diagnosed before liver transplantation for primary sclerosing cholangitis started upadacitinib 15 mg/day as anti-rejection therapy 3.7 years after the transplant. He was on prednisone 10 mg, mycophenolate mofetil and tacrolimus, with vedolizumab every 8 weeks for IBD control.

He had a prior episode of biopsy-confirmed rejection with ALT and alkaline phosphatase elevations following a prednisone taper. After upadacitinib was started prednisone was tapered from 10 to 5 mg/day and all other immunosuppressants were continued. He then developed elevated ALT of 41 U/L and alkaline phosphatase of 243 IU/L.

Given the prior rejection episode, allograft rejection was suspected and upadacitinib was discontinued after 5.5 months of exposure, with 8.5 months of total follow-up. COVID-19 is listed as an adverse event, and there were no life-threatening adverse events. Decisions followed multidisciplinary discussion with risks and benefits explained.
